topIssues.title: flaky test: `test_public_node_leaves_out_saved_loopback_record`
topIssues.author: sebastianst
topIssues.body:
CI run: https://app.circleci.com/workflow/199c962c-b686-4e7f-ad91-ecb4d4a3e213/job/b945eb89-2587-4657-adfd-d046f0debde2 (`rust-tests`, 2026-11-25)

Encountered on #24424, which does not touch `kona-disc`. The same Rust code passed `rust-tests` one push earlier; the failing push changed only Go test code.

The test is [`driver::tests::bootstore::test_public_node_leaves_out_saved_loopback_record`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/95dd69fb86e48587b2f5fbccc0b41ea3dfc58b78/rust/kona/crates/node/disc/src/driver/tests/bootstore.rs#L17-L36) in `kona-disc`.

```
thread 'driver::tests::bootstore::test_public_node_leaves_out_saved_loopback_record' panicked at kona/crates/node/disc/src/driver/tests/bootstore.rs:36:5:
assertion `left == right` failed: a public node dialed a saved loopback record
  left: [Enr { .. IpV4 UDP Socket: Some(1.1.1.1:9223), .. IpV4 TCP Socket: Some(1.1.1.1:9222), .. }, Enr { .. IpV4 UDP Socket: Some(1.1.1.1:9223), .. IpV4 TCP Socket: Some(1.1.1.1:9222), .. }]
 right: [Enr { .. IpV4 UDP Socket: Some(1.1.1.1:9223), .. IpV4 TCP Socket: Some(1.1.1.1:9222), .. }]
```

The loopback record was left out as intended. The batch holds the public record twice, with the same node ID both times. A likely cause: the test sets the store interval to 100 ms and assumes one hand-over is in the channel when it drains it, but on a loaded runner a second interval can fire before the drain, so the public record is handed over again.

🤖 *Co-created with Claude Fable 5.2*

topIssues.title: op-e2e/actions: build Amsterdam L1 blocks in the action-test L1 miner
topIssues.author: sebastianst
topIssues.body:
The action-test L1 miner builds L1 blocks itself with go-ethereum's block-processing functions: [`op-e2e/actions/helpers/l1_miner.go`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/36e225d1fd42ad77818665e24b6a2cf3b1c52f55/op-e2e/actions/helpers/l1_miner.go).

From Amsterdam on, an L1 block carries a block access list (EIP-7928) and a slot number. The miner builds neither. With the cutover to upstream go-ethereum (#24176) it fails with an explicit error when Amsterdam is active on L1, so no action test can run on an Amsterdam L1.

No action test activates L1 Amsterdam today.

## Task

- Build the block access list while the miner applies transactions and system calls, and set the header fields Amsterdam adds.
- Add an action test that runs on an Amsterdam L1, e.g. a batch submission and its derivation.

topIssues.title: flaky CI job: `cannon-prestate` fails when mise cannot fetch the jq release from the GitHub API
topIssues.author: sebastianst
topIssues.body:
https://circleci.com/gh/ethereum-optimism/optimism/5960421 (`cannon-prestate`, PR run, 2026-11-23)

Encountered on #24377, which touches only Go files. A rerun of the workflow passed without changes. The job also failed on develop and on other PRs within the same hour and passed on others; those logs were not read, so the same cause is likely but not confirmed.

The job runs `just reproducible-prestate` ([`.circleci/continue/main.yml#L2315`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/d6f6ff7d8c725c1206518881e131cb2897354d1b/.circleci/continue/main.yml#L2315)). The Docker build fails in [`cannon-repro.dockerfile#L52`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/d6f6ff7d8c725c1206518881e131cb2897354d1b/rust/kona/docker/fpvm-prestates/cannon-repro.dockerfile#L52), where mise fetches the jq release metadata from the GitHub API:

```
#21 [kona-build-env  7/23] RUN mise trust && mise install rust go just jq
#21 32.50 mise ERROR failed to install aqua:jqlang/jq@1.7.1
#21 32.50 mise ERROR error sending request for url (https://api.github.com/repos/jqlang/jq/releases/tags/jq-1.7.1)
#21 32.50 mise ERROR HTTP status client error (404 Not Found) for url (https://api.github.com/repos/jqlang/jq/releases/tags/jq-v1.7.1)
#21 ERROR: process "/bin/bash -c mise trust && mise install rust go just jq" did not complete successfully: exit code: 1
```

The request for the real tag (`jq-1.7.1`) fails in transport, mise falls back to a tag that does not exist (`jq-v1.7.1`), and the install fails. The build makes the request without a GitHub token and does not retry.

Impact: `ci-gate` fails with it, and `go-tests` and the `memory-all-*` acceptance jobs require this job, so they do not run at all in the affected workflow.

Possible fixes: retry the `mise install` step in a bounded loop, as [`docs/ai/docker.md`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/d6f6ff7d8c725c1206518881e131cb2897354d1b/docs/ai/docker.md) asks for every external fetch, or install jq in this image without a GitHub API call.

🤖 *Co-created with Claude Fable 5.2*

topIssues.title: flaky test: `TestL2ReorgAfterL1Reorg/unsafe_reorg`
topIssues.author: sebastianst
topIssues.body:
https://circleci.com/gh/ethereum-optimism/optimism/5964603 (`memory-all-opn-op-reth-fusaka`, merge queue run, 2026-11-24)

Encountered in the merge queue for #24377, which changes op-deployer intent parsing and removes an unused op-node helper. The test passed on both PR runs of that branch and on the re-queued run.

```
l2_reorgs_after_l1_reorg_test.go:166: INFO [11-24|15:32:54.176] L2 chain progressed, pointing to newer L1 block ref=cc7307..49d644:40 ref_origin=742ca4..58fdfc:28 divergence=f2c565..4acdea:21 scope=/TestL2ReorgAfterL1Reorg/unsafe_reorg
assertions.go:388:
    Error Trace: op-acceptance-tests/tests/interop/reorgs/l2_reorgs_after_l1_reorg_test.go:36
                 op-acceptance-tests/tests/interop/reorgs/l2_reorgs_after_l1_reorg_test.go:183
                 op-acceptance-tests/tests/interop/reorgs/l2_reorgs_after_l1_reorg_test.go:38
    Error:       Should be false
    Test:        TestL2ReorgAfterL1Reorg/unsafe_reorg
    Messages:    Previous unsafe block should have been reorged
```

The failing assertion is [`l2_reorgs_after_l1_reorg_test.go#L36`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/d6f6ff7d8c725c1206518881e131cb2897354d1b/op-acceptance-tests/tests/interop/reorgs/l2_reorgs_after_l1_reorg_test.go#L36): the unsafe head captured before the L1 reorg was still canonical on the L2 EL after the reorg had been recovered.

A possible cause, not verified: the test assumes that the unsafe head captured at [`#L31`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/d6f6ff7d8c725c1206518881e131cb2897354d1b/op-acceptance-tests/tests/interop/reorgs/l2_reorgs_after_l1_reorg_test.go#L31) has an L1 origin at or after the divergence block ([`#L100`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/d6f6ff7d8c725c1206518881e131cb2897354d1b/op-acceptance-tests/tests/interop/reorgs/l2_reorgs_after_l1_reorg_test.go#L100)). If the sequencer's L1 origin lags the L1 tip by more than the reorg depth at that moment, the block does not depend on a reorged L1 block and stays canonical. The job log does not show the origin of the captured block, so this is a lead only.

topPRs.title: lokahi,kona-node: proof of concept for nodes following a separate interop verifier
topPRs.author: sebastianst
topPRs.body:
**Proof of concept, not for merge.** Opened as a draft for CI feedback. Plan and progress are in #24423.

Unifying the CL and EL into one node per chain does not fit a supernode that embeds each chain's consensus node. This checks the alternative: lokahi runs as a separate interop verifier, and each chain's kona-node derives for itself and takes its safe head, finalized head and denied blocks from lokahi over RPC.

What is in here:
- lokahi: verification, invalidation and replacement, a durable store, L1 reorg handling and finality, and op-supernode's `superroot_atTimestamp` and `supernode_syncStatus` in the same wire format.
- kona-node: the authority client (one call returns an epoch, both heads and the denied blocks), block replacement, the undo when lokahi's epoch changes, op-node's handling of unsafe payloads around a denied block, and op-node's block-building RPC for the L2 test sequencer.
- op-devstack: `DEVSTACK_SUPERNODE_KIND=lokahi` runs the supernode presets on lokahi with a kona-node per chain; a preset with a sequencer, a source node and a follower per chain; a mode that runs each chain as one op-reth process with embedded kona (the commit of #24407, cherry-picked).

No effect on users: kona-node behaves as before unless `--interop.authority-rpc` is set, and lokahi is not released.

What CI should tell us: the kona-node acceptance job now runs the supernode presets on lokahi, with the op-node job on op-supernode as the control. The proofs presets run on lokahi here for the first time, so failures there are expected until they are triaged. CI has no job for the `op-reth` mode.

🤖 *Co-created with Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2*

topPRs.title: op-node,kona,op-acceptance-tests: add a derivation parity suite
topPRs.author: nonsense
topPRs.body:
kona-node is replacing op-node, and on some L1 data the two clients derive different safe chains, or one halts where the other continues. The data in question is batches, deposit and system config logs, and L1 block headers, plus the L2 blocks a node reads back on a reset. Until now these differences were known only from issue reports, with nothing to show which are still live. This PR adds a suite that gives both clients the same input, compares what each derives from it, and pins every difference it finds. A fix to either client then fails a test until the difference is taken off the list. `just derivation-parity-report` in `rust/kona/tests` prints how many cases each layer runs and every difference that remains.

There is no effect on users: the PR adds tests, test helpers and a local recipe. No client code changes.

Today the suite runs 130 cases: 78 agree and 52 differ, in 20 distinct ways.

<details><summary>The 20 differences</summary>

| Difference | Cases | Layers |
|---|---:|---|
| Span batch fee fields above 128 bits: kona keeps only the low 128 bits, op-node keeps the full value | 10 | vectors, proof, node |
| Span batch that fails span-batch derivation: kona drops the rest of its channel, op-node drops only that batch | 6 | vectors, proof |
| Brotli channel with a format error: kona discards the batches decoded before the error, op-node keeps them | 5 | vectors, proof |
| Span batch before Delta: kona passes it on for batch validation to drop, op-node drops it in the channel reader | 1 | vectors |
| L1-info blob base fee: kona uses built-in Cancun, Prague and Osaka blob parameters, op-node reads them from the L1 chain config | 3 | vectors |
| Pectra blob schedule override: kona drops it once L1 activates Osaka or a BPO fork, op-node applies it whatever L1 fork is active | 1 | vectors |
| Invalid Ecotone fee scalar in the system config: kona builds the L1-info deposit, op-node halts derivation | 2 | vectors |
| L1-info calldata in another fork's layout: kona decodes it, op-node rejects it | 6 | vectors |
| L1-info calldata with non-zero padding: kona ignores the padding, op-node rejects it | 3 | vectors |
| L1-info base fee above 64 bits or blob base fee above 128 bits: kona keeps only the low bits, op-node keeps the full value | 3 | vectors |
| TransactionDeposited data with non-zero padding: kona halts derivation, op-node accepts the deposit | 1 | vectors |
| TransactionDeposited data with an extra word after the opaque data: kona accepts the deposit, op-node halts derivation | 1 | vectors |
| TransactionDeposited from or to topic with non-zero padding: kona halts derivation, op-node accepts the deposit | 2 | vectors |
| EIP-1559 params update with a zero denominator or elasticity: kona applies it, op-node rejects it | 2 | vectors |
| EIP-1559 params update with non-zero padding: kona rejects it, op-node applies it | 1 | vectors |
| ConfigUpdate log with more than three topics: kona applies it, op-node rejects it | 1 | vectors |
| ConfigUpdate type with non-zero high bytes: kona reads the low bytes and applies it, op-node rejects it | 1 | vectors |
| Pre-Holocene L2 block with non-empty extraData: kona rebuilds its system config, op-node rejects the block | 1 | vectors |
| Holocene activating in the same L1 block as an earlier fork: kona switches to the Holocene derivation stages, op-node keeps the pre-Holocene stages | 1 | proof |
| A derived payload the engine rejects near Holocene activation: kona retries the rejected payload, op-node replaces it with a deposits-only block | 1 | node |

</details>

The suite pins today's behaviour and takes no side. Where the spec decides which client is right, the fix belongs to that client. Where the spec is silent, it needs a ruling first.

The suite has three layers, and each compares a different output.

**Vectors** call one derivation step directly, in each client. op-node writes each case's input and its own output to `rust/kona/crates/protocol/derive/testdata/parity_vectors.json`. kona-derive's `parity` test runs the same inputs and compares its output with op-node's. This layer finds the exact function that differs. It covers six steps:

| Step | Input | Output compared |
|---|---|---|
| Channel reader | One channel's bytes, as the channel bank hands them on, and the L1 origin's timestamp | The batches read from the channel, in order and field by field, and whether reading stops with an error |
| L1-info deposit | The system config, sequence number, L1 origin header, L2 block timestamp and L1 chain config | The encoded L1-info deposit transaction, or an error |
| L1-info decoding | The calldata of an L2 block's L1-info deposit, and the block's timestamp | The decoded fields, encoded again in the layout they were decoded from, or an error |
| Deposit log | A `TransactionDeposited` log, with its block hash and log index | The encoded deposit transaction, or an error |
| System config log | A system config, an L1 block timestamp, and a successful L1 receipt with one log | The system config after the receipt is applied |
| System config from an L2 block | An L2 block's number, timestamp, gas limit, extraData and L1-info deposit | The system config rebuilt from the block, as on a pipeline reset, or an error |

Each input also names the rollup config to use. The file stores each config once.

**Proof:** the input is crafted batch data posted to L1 in an action test, such as a span batch that raises a transaction's fee above 128 bits. op-node derives a safe chain from it in process. The output is kona-client's verdict on two claims for the L2 block at which the clients diverge. One is op-node's output root. The other is the claim for the chain kona derives: its output root, or the claim that the block cannot be derived.

**Node:** op-node and kona-node run side by side in devstack and derive from the same L1. The input is the batches posted there: the honest batcher's in the control test, crafted ones in the others. The output is the safe head each node records for an L1 block, read through `optimism_safeHeadAtL1Block`. The control test compares the two nodes' whole safe head databases. This is the only layer that reaches kona-node's engine, which kona-client does not run.

Points the diff does not make obvious:
- A system config output is compared by the values derivation reads, not by how the config stores them, so that two layouts with the same values do not count as a difference. Those values are the batcher address, overhead, scalar, gas limit, EIP-1559 parameters, operator fee, minimum base fee and DA footprint gas scalar. A zero DA footprint gas scalar is read as its default. L1-info decoding compares the encoded fields rather than the calldata for the same reason.
- The Go vector test builds every case's input again and checks it against the committed file. It then runs op-node on the committed inputs and checks its outputs. The input check skips a channel case's channel bytes, so a compressor upgrade does not fail it.
- kona's output on each vector case that differs is pinned too, in `parity_kona_differences.json`. A change in *how* kona differs therefore also fails, until its description is updated.
- A crafted proof case also checks that kona-client accepts the claim of the chain kona derives. kona-host rejects any claim when the client errors, so the rejection of op-node's claim alone does not prove the chains differ.
- Each crafted case has a control that differs only by the crafted change.
- The node-layer tests start both clients themselves. They therefore skip under `DEVSTACK_L2CL_KIND=kona-node`, where they would only repeat the op-node job.

Review:
- `go-code-reviewer` (twice), `rust-code-reviewer` and `ci-config-reviewer` ran. Their findings are fixed, except those below.
- The derivation, deposit, SP1 cost and safe-head-database reviewers are not run: the diff changes no client behaviour, and adds no dependency to a guest crate.
- The security review is still owed before this leaves draft.

Deferred, as follow-ups that change code or CI outside this PR:
- **Duplicate batch-posting step:** `dsl.PostBatches` duplicates the batch-posting helper of the SDM acceptance tests, which could wrap it.
- **Copied setup:** the side-by-side system setup is copied from `safedb_parity`, and could become a preset.
- **CI routing gap:** CI runs the proof layer only when `rust/` or `op-e2e/` changes. A PR that changes only op-node's side of a difference therefore merges green, and fails on develop. The docs now say to run the recipe for such a change. Routing `op-node/rollup/` changes to the rust e2e jobs is a separate CI change.

Not covered by a case yet:
- a channel flush reaching the channel assembler (no known way to trigger it);
- the stage origin after a reset to a pre-Holocene base near genesis;
- a batcher signature that cannot be recovered, when the batcher address is zero;
- the reset walk-back channel timeout across Granite (op-node's side needs a reset, so this belongs in the node layer).

Local runs: the vectors and the Go and Rust unit tests ran on this branch. The proof and node layers passed locally, but on `op-reth-test-engine`, `kona-node` and `op-reth` binaries built from other branches, because there was no disk space to build them here. This PR's CI is their first run on binaries built from this branch.

topPRs.title: docs/public-docs: run the docs preview and tooling on mise-pinned bun
topPRs.author: pauldowman
topPRs.body:
Previewing docs.optimism.io locally needed Node, pnpm and a globally installed `mint` CLI, none of which the repo pins. The documented `pnpm dev` failed out of the box, and `pnpm install` itself failed under the pinned pnpm because of a placeholder `pnpm-workspace.yaml`. `just public-docs` now installs dependencies and serves the preview using only the `bun` and `just` pinned in `mise.toml`, and the generators and lints run on the same `bun`.

- **Effect on contributors:** `pnpm …` commands become `bun run …`, and Node, pnpm and tsx are no longer needed. No effect on the published site: Mintlify deploys through its GitHub app and doesn't run `package.json` scripts, and no CI job installs the docs' JS dependencies.
- **`mint` is an exact-pinned devDependency** of `docs/public-docs`, so `bun.lock` locks its whole dependency tree, rather than pinning a `bunx mint@<version>` call in the root justfile.
- **More advisories become visible; the risk is not new.** `bun audit` on the docs package goes from 8 to 43 advisories, almost all in versions that `mint` pins exactly. Contributors already ran these same packages through a global `mint` install or `npx`; the repo just had no record of them, so nothing could flag them. Exposure is a localhost preview, and the fix is bumping `mint`, which Renovate can now see (expect frequent `mint` bump PRs). `sharp` is overridden to 0.35.5 because `mint` pins the vulnerable 0.33.5, restoring the protection #22733 added.
- **`react`/`react-dom` removed:** they were unused (Mintlify supplies React at runtime; `components/HomeCard.tsx` only imports types), and their React 18 was loaded instead of `mint`'s React 19, which crashed `mint dev`.
- **Accepted:** the existing `minimatch >=9.0.7` override forces minimatch 10 onto Spectral, a `mint` dependency expecting ^3. Spectral only reaches that code for rulesets with `overrides`, and this site has no OpenAPI or AsyncAPI specs.
- Tutorials that tell readers to use pnpm, npx or tsx for their own projects are unchanged.
- `lint:nav` (887 errors) and `lint:reference` (3 errors) fail identically on `develop`; not addressed here.

Reviews: `ci-config-reviewer` and `deletion-reviewer` ran on the branch; their findings are fixed. `/op:security-reviewer` has not run yet and must run before this is marked ready. Unconfirmed: whether GitHub's dependency graph and the `dependency-review` check parse `bun.lock`.

topPRs.title: op-node,op-service,kona-protocol: pin L1 info deposits, block hashes and RPC tx decoding with real chain data
topPRs.author: sebastianst
topPRs.body:
Tests and fixtures only. Three consensus-critical Go paths were pinned thinly or only against their own output, so a decoder regression like the one fixed in #24350 passed every unit test. Each path is now pinned against real chain data.

- **L1-info deposit calldata**: op-node and kona assert the same vectors from one fixture file, so the two cannot drift apart. The vectors are tx 0 of real OP Mainnet and Base blocks for Bedrock, Ecotone, Isthmus and Jovian, plus synthetic ones for a non-zero operator fee and near-maximum Jovian fields, which no live chain has. Both suites check calldata, source hash and deposit tx hash, and decode the calldata back.
- **`CheckBlockHash`**: a table over real op-reth payloads, one per payload shape from pre-Canyon to Karst. Each row also changes one header input and must then mismatch. Until now the gossip and batcher tests computed the expected hash with the function under test.
- **`RawTransaction` JSON decoding**: real L1 blocks covering tx types 0–4, including Ethereum mainnet block 26268195 with the authorization `yParity` 28 behind #24350, and an OP Mainnet block with legacy, EIP-1559 and EIP-7702 user txs. `TestBlockJSON` now checks every tx hash.

No effect on users.

For the reviewer:
- The two mainnet block fixtures are large (roughly a quarter megabyte each). The second one exists for type-1 coverage; no smaller block with a type-1 tx turned up.
- Both mainnet blocks contain a transaction whose calldata is a solicitation text addressed to wallet owners. It is inert test data, but it cannot be removed without breaking the tx root.
- Not covered: a type-1 tx on L2, a real L2 user deposit with non-zero mint (the existing devnet fixtures pin mint and contract-creation deposits), and kona's production deposit builder, which the Rust test would only reach after a small refactor.

Reviews run: Go review, Rust review, security review.

🤖 *Co-created with Claude Fable 5.2*

topPRs.title: op-zk-proposer: extend and defend only the anchor and its own games
topPRs.author: digorithm
topPRs.body:
The proposer adopted the highest valid game as its parent whoever created it, and defended, resolved and closed any game whose prestate it could load. Every foreign ancestor puts the games we build on it at risk, and third parties control how many exist and how long they span (audit findings 3, 5 and 11; also the unsafe-L1-head game that is challenged at the last minute). After this PR the proposer extends only the anchor or games it owns, and defends only games it owns. This reverses the position in #22111, agreed with @pauldowman and Gustavo after the audit.

Effect on operators:
- A game is owned when its creator is the signer or listed in the new `OP_ZK_PROPOSER_OWNED_CREATORS`, and its prestate is known. Set the variable to the old signer when rotating the key, and remove it once the anchor has moved past the old signer's last game. Unset is the normal state.
- Upgrade step: this version no longer defends foreign games, including a foreign parent of an in-flight signer game. Before deploying, check that no in-progress signer game has an unresolved foreign ancestor; if one does, list that creator in `OP_ZK_PROPOSER_OWNED_CREATORS` until the anchor has moved past it.
- The span of games built on the head is now capped. While the proposer keeps up, a game spans one proposal interval. When it falls two or more intervals behind (downtime, or games that take longer than an interval to create or, in fast finality mode, to prove), a game spans up to the new `OP_ZK_PROPOSER_MAX_PROPOSAL_SPAN_INTERVALS` intervals (default 4). Before this PR the catch-up game spanned the whole gap. Bond and prove duration must cover the configured maximum.
- `OP_ZK_PROPOSER_PROPOSAL_INTERVAL_SECONDS=0` now fails at startup. It used to mean "propose at the safe head".
- Foreign games are no longer resolved or closed by the proposer. op-challenger or their creator does it. Until then, `op_dispute_mon_zk_games_pending_lifecycle_action` counts them, and an owned game created on a foreign parent before this change cannot resolve. Claims stay credit-driven, so challenger bonds already earned on foreign games are still claimed.
- The info log "Discovered game created by another proposer" is gone.

Reasons the diff does not show:
- Foreign games stay cached as untrusted records because tracking the anchor needs their factory index; without them an anchor move to a foreign game rescans the factory.
- Head selection follows a chain down to the anchor, a root, or an owned game that resolved `DefenderWins` (its ancestors can no longer lose). Anyone can move the anchor to a valid foreign game; without the `DefenderWins` stop, a restart that leaves our chain's root outside the discovery window made the whole chain fail the check.
- On a UUID collision with a foreign root while the anchor is not a ZK game, the proposer now walks one second like on the normal path instead of waiting for the next interval. The wait relied on the foreign root becoming our head; without that, one copy per interval would stop creation.
- When the registry rejects the head's chain, the fallback root keeps the head's timestamp and can span more than one interval. Recomputing it from the anchor livelocks. With no anchor game registered, a broken chain likewise restarts from the last head's timestamp.

Accepted risk (security review finding): a UUID does not include the creator, so a third party can create our next game first. The proposer walks one second and retries, so stopping creation takes a copy of every attempt, each with a bond that comes back to the attacker (unchallenged, or self-challenged). The README states this. A follow-up tracks a fix.

Closes https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/proofs-team/issues/48

Review findings dismissed or deferred:
- Make `proposal_interval_seconds` a `NonZeroU64`: `from_env`, the only production constructor, rejects zero, and devstack already does.
- Replace the candidate tuples with a struct: the tuple shape predates this PR.
- A creation guard whose game never reaches the cache (a create dropped by a reorg deeper than the 3-confirmation receipt wait and never mined again) can stop creation until a restart. If the dropped game spanned one interval, the bounded catch-up plans past it once the proposer is two intervals behind. If it was a full-span catch-up game, the next plan never exceeds the guarded timestamp, so creation stops until a restart. Deferred to a follow-up issue.
- The registry-rejection fallback can still skip a root that would not advance a new registry's anchor root, if that root is at or above head plus the maximum span. This needs a registry whose starting root is ahead of our newest proposal.
- No acceptance test asserts the prover-credit claim after defending a listed creator's game; the scenario test `foreign_game_proven_by_the_signer_is_claimed_after_a_third_party_resolves_it` covers the claim path.

The ZK acceptance suite was not run locally; it runs in CI. `kona-sp1-cost-reviewer` does not apply because no guest code changes.
